summary: Implemented HTTPS on node1:8443 via Ansible run from control node2. nginx serves TLS on 8443 using a self-signed cert (90-day validity, CN/SAN=node1.cluster.local + node IP) stored behind stable symlinks in /etc/nginx/ssl/live/. A systemd oneshot service + hourly timer (cert-renew.service/.timer) runs /usr/local/sbin/renew-selfsigned-cert.sh, which checks expiry with `openssl x509 -checkend` (30-day threshold), regenerates the cert into a timestamped archive dir, atomically swaps the live symlinks, then runs `nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx` for a graceful, zero-downtime reload that picks up the new cert for new TLS handshakes while existing connections finish normally. node1 (Ubuntu 16.04/Xenial) had only Python 2.7/3.5, incompatible with modern ansible-core 2.20 modules; built Python 3.9.19 from source on node1 and pointed ansible_python_interpreter at it to make the playbook fully idiomatic (apt/file/template/systemd modules), only falling back to raw `command` for apt install (python3-apt unavailable for the custom interpreter) and swapping openssl's unsupported `-addext` for an inline OpenSSL config file (OpenSSL 1.0.2g on Xenial). Verified end-to-end: forced a renewal while a continuous curl loop hit the endpoint from node2 — all 81 requests returned HTTP 200 with zero failures, and a subsequent TLS handshake fingerprint matched the new cert, proving hot pickup without downtime. Playbook re-run is idempotent (changed=0). Completed the mandatory restart protocol: node1 and node2 were each rebooted one at a time via `shutdown -r now`, boot_id changed on both, and post-restart nginx/timer were active+enabled with the same cert still valid and HTTPS still answering 200 (locally and remotely), and node2's ansible control capability (and a full re-run) worked after its own reboot.
